decks.title: Redox Reactions — Part 1: Oxidation, reduction and oxidation number
goals: State the classical and electron-transfer definitions of oxidation and reduction
Assign oxidation numbers using the rules, including fractional values, peroxides and superoxides
Identify the oxidising and reducing agents in a reaction from changes in oxidation number
Use Stock notation and distinguish oxidation number from valence

slides.heading: Redox Reactions
slides.body_md: Part 1 — oxidation and reduction always happen together. We learn to follow the electrons with a bookkeeping number.

rows: The metal at the negative terminal

visual.alt: Table of everyday redox processes, what is oxidised and why each matters

slides.narration: Welcome. Rusting, burning fuel, a battery running down and bleach removing a stain all have one thing in common: electrons move from one substance to another. In this part we define oxidation and reduction, and learn the rules for oxidation numbers, which let us track those electrons even in molecules.

slides.heading: The classical view
slides.body_md: Early chemists defined the terms by what happens to oxygen, hydrogen or other elements. Oxidation and reduction are **opposite changes in the same reaction**, for example $\ce{H2S + Cl2 -> 2HCl + S}$, where hydrogen sulfide loses hydrogen.

visual.alt: Table of the classical definitions of oxidation and reduction

slides.narration: In the classical view, oxidation means adding oxygen, removing hydrogen, adding an electronegative element or removing an electropositive one. Reduction is the reverse. When hydrogen sulfide reacts with chlorine, the sulfide loses hydrogen and is oxidised, while chlorine gains hydrogen and is reduced. The two changes cannot happen separately.

slides.heading: The electron-transfer view
slides.body_md: **Oxidation** is loss of electrons; **reduction** is gain of electrons. The substance that gains electrons (and is itself reduced) is the **oxidising agent**; the one that loses electrons is the **reducing agent**. Each reaction splits into two **half-reactions**.

visual.alt: Table splitting the reaction of zinc with copper two ions into oxidation and reduction half-reactions

slides.narration: The modern definition follows electrons. Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain. When zinc is placed in a copper sulfate solution, each zinc atom gives two electrons and each copper ion takes two. Zinc is the reducing agent, because it supplies electrons, and the copper ion is the oxidising agent, because it takes them.

slides.heading: Rules for oxidation numbers
slides.body_md: The **oxidation number** (ON) is the charge an atom would have if all bonding electrons were assigned to the more electronegative atom. Apply the rules in this order of priority.

rows: An atom in an element has ON 0
A simple ion has ON equal to its charge
Sum of ONs equals the charge on the species

visual.alt: Table of the rules for assigning oxidation numbers with examples

slides.narration: Oxidation numbers follow a short list of rules. Atoms in an element are zero. A simple ion has an oxidation number equal to its charge. The numbers in a species always add up to its charge. Alkali metals are plus one, alkaline earth metals plus two, fluorine minus one, hydrogen usually plus one, and oxygen usually minus two, with a few exceptions such as peroxides.

slides.heading: Oxidation numbers of manganese
slides.body_md: One element can take many oxidation numbers. Going **up** the ladder is oxidation (ON rises, electrons lost); going **down** is reduction. Permanganate, at +7, has manganese in its highest state.

slides.narration: Manganese is a good example of an element with many oxidation numbers. The metal is zero. In the manganese two ion it is plus two, in manganese dioxide plus four, in manganate plus six, and in permanganate plus seven. Moving up the ladder means electrons are lost, which is oxidation, and moving down means electrons are gained, which is reduction.

slides.heading: Quick check: oxidation number
slides.body_md: Find the oxidation number of an element in a compound.
slides.narration: Quick check. Write the sum of all the oxidation numbers and set it equal to the charge of the species.

slides.heading: Worked example: oxidation numbers
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the oxidation number of (i) Cr in $\ce{K2Cr2O7}$, (ii) S in $\ce{S4O6^2-}$, (iii) Fe in $\ce{Fe3O4}$.

**(i)** Let Cr be $x$: $2(+1) + 2x + 7(-2) = 0$, so $2x = 12$ and $x = +6$.

**(ii)** $4x + 6(-2) = -2$, so $4x = 10$ and $x = +2.5$ (an average value).

**(iii)** $3x + 4(-2) = 0$, so $3x = 8$ and $x \approx +2.67$ (average of Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺).

visual.alt: Table of the working for the oxidation numbers of chromium, sulfur and iron

slides.narration: Let the unknown oxidation number be x and add everything up. In potassium dichromate, two plus two x minus fourteen equals zero, so chromium is plus six. In the tetrathionate ion, four x minus twelve equals minus two, so sulfur averages two and a half. In the iron oxide, three x minus eight equals zero, so iron averages two and two thirds.

slides.heading: Fractional values, peroxides and superoxides
slides.body_md: A fractional ON is an **average** over atoms of the same element in different environments. Oxygen has ON −1 in peroxides (O–O link), −½ in superoxides and +2 in $\ce{OF2}$, where fluorine is more electronegative.

rows: Superoxide ion O₂⁻, two O share −1
One O at −2 and four O at −1 (two peroxo groups)

visual.alt: Table of special oxidation numbers in peroxides, superoxides, an oxygen fluoride, carbon suboxide and chromium pentoxide

slides.narration: Some cases need care. In hydrogen peroxide the oxygen atoms are joined to each other, so each is minus one. In a superoxide such as potassium superoxide, the oxygen is minus one half. In oxygen difluoride, fluorine wins the electrons, so oxygen is plus two. Fractions simply mean an average over atoms in different environments.

slides.heading: Spotting a redox reaction
slides.body_md: A reaction is redox if **some oxidation number changes**. The species whose ON rises is oxidised (the reducing agent); the species whose ON falls is reduced (the oxidising agent).

visual.alt: Table of four reactions with the atoms whose oxidation numbers rise or fall

slides.narration: To decide if a reaction is redox, write the oxidation numbers of each element before and after. If any of them changes, it is redox. The atom whose number goes up has been oxidised, so its compound is the reducing agent. The atom whose number goes down has been reduced, so its compound is the oxidising agent. If nothing changes, as in neutralisation, it is not redox.

slides.heading: Worked example: oxidant and reductant
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** For $\ce{2PbS + 3O2 -> 2PbO + 2SO2}$, find the oxidising and reducing agents.

**Step 1.** ON of S: $-2$ in PbS and $+4$ in $\ce{SO2}$ (rises by 6).

**Step 2.** ON of O: $0$ in $\ce{O2}$ and $-2$ in the products (falls by 2).

**Step 3.** Pb stays at $+2$. So PbS (sulfur) is the **reducing agent** and $\ce{O2}$ is the **oxidising agent**.

visual.alt: Table of oxidation number changes of sulfur, oxygen and lead in the roasting of lead sulfide

slides.narration: Write each element before and after. Sulfur goes from minus two to plus four, so it is oxidised and lead sulfide is the reducing agent. Oxygen goes from zero to minus two, so it is reduced and oxygen gas is the oxidising agent. Lead stays at plus two throughout, so it is just a spectator.

slides.heading: Quick check: oxidising agent
slides.body_md: Decide which species is the oxidising agent.
slides.narration: Quick check. Look for the atom whose oxidation number falls.

visual.caption: Stepwise oxidation of carbon: each step removes two electrons.

slides.narration: Carbon shows a wide range. In methane it is minus four. Replacing hydrogen atoms by oxygen atoms moves it up in steps of two: methanol minus two, methanal zero, methanoic acid plus two, and finally carbon dioxide plus four. Each step is an oxidation and loses two electrons per carbon atom. Burning a fuel completes the whole climb.

slides.heading: Oxidation number, valence and Stock notation
slides.body_md: **Valence** is the number of bonds an atom forms (no sign); **ON** carries a sign and can be zero or a fraction. In methane and methanal, carbon has valence 4 in both but ON −4 and 0. **Stock notation** writes the metal ON in Roman numerals: iron(III) oxide.

visual.alt: Table of formulas, metal oxidation numbers and Stock names

slides.narration: Do not confuse valence with oxidation number. Valence counts bonds and has no sign. Oxidation number has a sign and can be zero or a fraction. Carbon forms four bonds in both methane and methanal, but its oxidation numbers differ. Stock notation puts the oxidation number of the metal in Roman numerals in brackets, as in iron three oxide.

slides.heading: Common oxidising and reducing agents
slides.body_md: An element in its **highest** oxidation state can only be an oxidising agent; in its **lowest** only a reducing agent; in an **intermediate** state it can be either (for example $\ce{H2O2}$, $\ce{SO2}$).

visual.alt: Table of common oxidising and reducing agents with their usual products

slides.narration: An element at its highest oxidation state can only gain electrons, so it can only be an oxidising agent. At its lowest state it can only lose them, so it is only a reducing agent. At an intermediate state it can do either. Permanganate and dichromate in acid are strong oxidising agents, while metals, iodide and hydrogen sulfide are common reducing agents.

slides.heading: Quick check: highest and lowest states
slides.body_md: Decide which species cannot act as a reducing agent.
slides.narration: Quick check. Ask whether the element can still lose electrons.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Oxidation: loss of electrons, rise in ON; reduction: gain of electrons, fall in ON; they occur together.
Reducing agent loses electrons and is oxidised; oxidising agent gains electrons and is reduced.
ON rules: element 0; ion = charge; sum = overall charge; H +1; O −2 with peroxide (−1), superoxide (−½) and OF₂ (+2) exceptions.
Fractional ON is an average; ON differs from valence; Stock notation gives the metal ON in Roman numerals.
Highest ON: oxidant only; lowest ON: reductant only; intermediate: either.

visual.alt: Summary table of redox terms

slides.narration: Let us sum up. Oxidation is loss of electrons and a rise in oxidation number. Reduction is gain and a fall. The reducing agent is oxidised and the oxidising agent is reduced. Follow the rules to assign oxidation numbers, remember the exceptions for peroxides and superoxides, and use the highest and lowest oxidation states to judge what a species can do.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Write the sum of all oxidation numbers equal to the charge before solving for x.
Check for peroxide or superoxide links before assuming oxygen is −2.
Name the agent as the species (the compound), not the atom, and say what happens to it.
Quote fractional ONs as averages and explain with the structure when asked.
Show the ON change for the atom, not the whole formula.

rows: Check for O–O bonds and fluorides
Reducing agent is the atom that is reduced
Valence and ON are the same
ON has a sign and may be a fraction
Sum of ONs is zero for an ion

visual.alt: Table of four common slips in oxidation number questions and their fixes

slides.narration: Some exam tips. Always set the sum of oxidation numbers equal to the charge. Look for peroxide links before using minus two for oxygen. Remember that the reducing agent is the species that is oxidised. And when you meet a fraction, say that it is an average over atoms in different environments.

goals: Classify redox reactions as combination, decomposition, displacement and disproportionation
Describe a Daniell cell as redox split between two electrodes
Balance redox equations by the oxidation-number and half-reaction methods in acidic and basic medium
Use mole ratios from balanced redox equations in permanganate titrations

slides.heading: Types and balancing
slides.body_md: Part 2 — four patterns that cover most redox reactions, and two systematic ways to balance any of them.

rows: One species gives two products at higher and lower ON

visual.alt: Table of four types of redox reaction with general pattern and an example

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Redox reactions fall into four common types: combination, decomposition, displacement and disproportionation. After meeting each, we learn two methods to balance redox equations, the oxidation number method and the half reaction method, and we finish with a titration that uses them.

slides.heading: Combination and decomposition
slides.body_md: A **combination** reaction is redox if an element takes part; a **decomposition** is redox if an element is formed. Reactions between compounds with no ON change, such as $\ce{CaO + CO2 -> CaCO3}$, are **not** redox.

visual.alt: Table of combination and decomposition reactions showing which are redox

slides.narration: A combination reaction is a redox reaction when one of the reactants is a free element, as when nitrogen and hydrogen make ammonia. A decomposition is redox when a free element appears among the products, as when potassium chlorate gives oxygen. But limestone breaking down, or lime combining with carbon dioxide, changes no oxidation numbers, so these are not redox.

slides.heading: Displacement reactions
slides.body_md: In a **displacement** reaction an atom or ion is replaced by another that is a stronger reducing agent (metals) or stronger oxidising agent (non-metals). Activity series (decreasing): K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, **H**, Cu, Ag, Au.

visual.alt: Table of four kinds of displacement reaction with examples

slides.narration: In a displacement reaction a more reactive element pushes out a less reactive one. A metal above copper in the activity series displaces copper from its solution. A metal above hydrogen displaces hydrogen from an acid. Among the halogens, chlorine displaces bromine and iodine, but not the other way round. Even oxygen in water is displaced by fluorine.

slides.heading: A Daniell cell: redox in two vessels
slides.body_md: Put the oxidation and reduction half-reactions in **separate vessels** joined by a wire and a salt bridge: electrons now flow through the wire and can do work. Oxidation at the **anode**; reduction at the **cathode**.

slides.narration: In a Daniell cell, zinc sits in zinc sulfate on one side and copper sits in copper sulfate on the other. slides.narration: In disproportionation, one substance is oxidised and reduced at the same time. Hydrogen peroxide does this when it forms water and oxygen. Chlorine does it in alkali. Starting at zero, chlorine goes down to chloride at minus one and up to hypochlorite at plus one in the cold, or to chlorate at plus five when hot. White phosphorus does the same in alkali, forming phosphine and hypophosphite.

slides.heading: Balancing by the oxidation-number method
slides.body_md: Use the fact that **total increase in ON = total decrease in ON**. Work on whole atoms, equalise the changes with multipliers, then balance the other atoms.

nodes.label: Equalise total rise and fall with multipliers
Balance other atoms, O then H last

visual.alt: Flow chart of the oxidation number method of balancing a redox equation

slides.narration: The oxidation number method rests on one idea: what goes up in oxidation number must equal what goes down. Write the skeleton equation, assign oxidation numbers, find the atoms that change, and multiply so the total rise equals the total fall. Then balance the remaining atoms, leaving oxygen and hydrogen for last, and check atoms and charge.

slides.heading: Worked example: oxidation-number method
slides.body_md:
**(a) Balance** $\ce{Fe2O3 + CO -> Fe + CO2}$. Fe: $+3 \to 0$, a fall of 3 per atom, so 2 Fe fall by 6. C: $+2 \to +4$, a rise of 2. Multiplier 3 for CO and CO₂: $\ce{Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2}$.

**(b) Balance** $\ce{Cu + HNO3 -> Cu(NO3)2 + NO2 + H2O}$ (concentrated acid). Cu rises by 2; N (to NO₂) falls by 1, so 2 $\ce{NO2}$ per Cu. Add 2 nitrate for the salt: $\ce{Cu + 4HNO3 -> Cu(NO3)2 + 2NO2 + 2H2O}$.

visual.alt: Table of the steps of the oxidation number method for the reduction of iron oxide and for copper with concentrated nitric acid

slides.narration: For the iron oxide, each iron falls by three and there are two iron atoms, a total fall of six. Each carbon rises by two, so three carbon monoxide balance it. For copper with concentrated nitric acid, copper rises by two and each nitrogen falls by one, so two nitrogen dioxide appear per copper. Two more nitrates are needed for the salt, so four nitric acid are used.

slides.heading: Balancing by the half-reaction method
slides.body_md: Split the reaction into two half-reactions and balance each **atom by atom and charge by charge**. In **acidic** medium use $\ce{H2O}$ and $\ce{H+}$; for **basic** medium balance as in acid, then add $\ce{OH-}$ equal to the $\ce{H+}$ on **both** sides.

nodes.label: Balance atoms other than O and H
Multiply to equalise electrons and add
Basic medium: add OH⁻ to cancel H⁺

visual.alt: Flow chart of the half-reaction method for acidic and basic medium

slides.narration: In the half reaction method we balance oxidation and reduction separately. Balance every atom except oxygen and hydrogen, then oxygen with water, then hydrogen with hydrogen ions, and finally charge with electrons. Multiply so that the electrons match and add the two halves. For a basic solution, add hydroxide ions to both sides to cancel the hydrogen ions.

slides.heading: Worked example: acidic medium
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Balance $\ce{MnO4- + Fe^2+ -> Mn^2+ + Fe^3+}$ in acid.

**Reduction:** $\ce{MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- -> Mn^2+ + 4H2O}$

**Oxidation (×5):** $\ce{5Fe^2+ -> 5Fe^3+ + 5e-}$

**Add:** $\ce{MnO4- + 8H+ + 5Fe^2+ -> Mn^2+ + 5Fe^3+ + 4H2O}$. Charge: $-1 + 8 + 10 = +17$ on the left; $+2 + 15 = +17$ on the right.

visual.alt: Table of the two half-reactions and the sum for permanganate oxidising iron two in acid

slides.narration: Permanganate goes to manganese two. Four oxygens need four waters, which need eight hydrogen ions, and the charge needs five electrons. Iron two to iron three gives only one electron, so multiply it by five. Adding the halves, the electrons cancel and we get one permanganate with eight hydrogen ions and five iron ions. The charge is plus seventeen on both sides.

slides.heading: Quick check: half-reaction
slides.body_md: Complete a half-reaction in acidic medium.
slides.narration: Quick check. Balance oxygen with water, hydrogen with hydrogen ions, then charge with electrons.

slides.heading: Worked example: basic medium
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Balance $\ce{MnO4- + I- -> MnO2 + I2}$ in basic medium.

**Reduction:** $\ce{MnO4- + 2H2O + 3e- -> MnO2 + 4OH-}$

**Oxidation:** $\ce{2I- -> I2 + 2e-}$

**Multiply** the first by 2 and the second by 3, then add: $\ce{2MnO4- + 6I- + 4H2O -> 2MnO2 + 3I2 + 8OH-}$. Charge: $-2 - 6 = -8$ on both sides.

visual.alt: Table of the half-reactions and the sum for permanganate and iodide in basic medium

slides.narration: In basic solution permanganate is reduced to manganese dioxide. Written with water on the left and hydroxide on the right, it takes three electrons. Iodide loses two electrons per iodine molecule. Multiply by two and by three so six electrons are gained and lost, and add. The hydroxide appears on the right, and the charge is minus eight on both sides.

slides.heading: Redox titration with permanganate
slides.body_md: In acid, $\ce{MnO4-}$ takes **5** electrons and $\ce{Fe^2+}$ gives **1**, so **1 mol MnO₄⁻ reacts with 5 mol Fe²⁺**. Permanganate is its own indicator. Use dilute **sulfuric** acid, not hydrochloric or nitric acid.

The acid must be dilute sulfuric acid. Hydrochloric acid would itself be oxidised by permanganate, and nitric acid is itself an oxidising agent, so both would spoil the result.

slides.heading: Worked example: titration calculation
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** $25.0\ \text{mL}$ of an iron(II) solution needs $20.0\ \text{mL}$ of $0.0200\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ $\ce{KMnO4}$ in acid. Find the molarity of iron(II).

**Step 1.** $n(\text{MnO}_4^-) = 0.0200 \times \dfrac{20.0}{1000} = 4.00 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol}$.

**Step 2.** $n(\text{Fe}^{2+}) = 5 \times 4.00 \times 10^{-4} = 2.00 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}$.

**Step 3.** $c = \dfrac{2.00 \times 10^{-3}}{25.0/1000} = 0.0800\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Table of the quantities in the permanganate titration of iron two

slides.narration: First find the moles of permanganate used: the concentration times the volume in litres. Then multiply by five, because one permanganate oxidises five iron two ions. Finally divide the moles of iron by the volume of the sample in litres to get the concentration, about zero point zero eight zero moles per litre.

slides.narration: Let us sum up. Redox reactions can be classified as combination, decomposition, displacement and disproportionation. A cell separates oxidation and reduction. To balance, either equalise the changes in oxidation number or balance two half reactions, adding hydroxide for basic solutions. And a balanced equation gives the mole ratio for titrations, such as one permanganate to five iron two.

sections.heading: 1. Oxidation and reduction
sections.body_md:
**Classical view:** oxidation is addition of oxygen or an electronegative element, or removal of hydrogen or an electropositive element; reduction is the reverse. **Electron view:** oxidation is **loss** of electrons, reduction is **gain** of electrons (remember: OIL RIG).

The **oxidising agent** accepts electrons and is itself reduced; the **reducing agent** donates electrons and is itself oxidised. Every redox reaction is a pair of **half-reactions**; electrons lost equal electrons gained. For $\ce{Zn + Cu^2+ -> Zn^2+ + Cu}$: oxidation $\ce{Zn -> Zn^2+ + 2e-}$, reduction $\ce{Cu^2+ + 2e- -> Cu}$.

Gain of electrons; decrease in oxidation number.
The species that accepts electrons and is reduced.
The species that donates electrons and is oxidised.

sections.heading: 2. Oxidation number and its rules
sections.body_md:
The **oxidation number** is the hypothetical charge on an atom if all bonding electrons went to the more electronegative atom. Rules: (1) atoms in an element: 0; (2) simple ion: its charge; (3) the sum for a species equals its charge; (4) group 1 is +1, group 2 is +2, fluorine is −1; (5) hydrogen is +1 (−1 in metal hydrides); (6) oxygen is −2, but −1 in peroxides, −½ in superoxides, +2 in $\ce{OF2}$.

A fractional ON is an average (Fe in $\ce{Fe3O4}$ is +8/3; S in $\ce{S4O6^2-}$ is +5/2). ON is **not** the same as valence: ON has a sign, and can be zero or fractional. **Stock notation** gives the metal's ON in Roman numerals: iron(III) oxide, $\ce{Fe2O3}$.

sections.heading: 3. Identifying redox reactions and agents
sections.body_md:
A reaction is redox if any oxidation number changes. The species containing the atom whose ON **rises** is oxidised (the **reducing agent**); the species containing the atom whose ON **falls** is reduced (the **oxidising agent**). Neutralisation and precipitation reactions are not redox.

An element at its **highest** ON can only act as an oxidant ($\ce{MnO4-}$, $\ce{Cr2O7^2-}$, $\ce{ClO4-}$); at its **lowest** only as a reductant ($\ce{S^2-}$, $\ce{I-}$, $\ce{H2S}$); at an **intermediate** ON as either ($\ce{H2O2}$, $\ce{SO2}$, $\ce{HNO2}$).

key_terms.definition_md: An oxidation number between the highest and lowest the element can show; the species can be oxidised or reduced.

sections.heading: 4. Types of redox reactions
sections.body_md:
- **Combination:** $\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$ (redox only if a free element is involved).
- **Decomposition:** $\ce{2KClO3 -> 2KCl + 3O2}$ (redox if an element is formed; $\ce{CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2}$ is not).
- **Displacement:** a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one ($\ce{Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu}$) or hydrogen from an acid; a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one ($\ce{Cl2 + 2KBr -> 2KCl + Br2}$). Activity series: K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, H, Cu, Ag, Au.
- **Disproportionation:** the same element is both oxidised and reduced: $\ce{2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2}$; $\ce{Cl2 + 2OH- -> Cl- + ClO- + H2O}$ (cold, dilute alkali); $\ce{P4 + 3OH- + 3H2O -> PH3 + 3H2PO2-}$.

In a **Daniell cell** the zinc anode is oxidised, the copper cathode is reduced, and electrons flow from zinc to copper through the wire; a salt bridge completes the circuit.

key_terms.definition_md: A reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound.
A redox reaction in which the same element in one species is simultaneously oxidised and reduced.

sections.heading: 5. Balancing redox equations
sections.body_md:
**Oxidation-number method:** write the skeleton, assign ON, find the total rise and fall, multiply to equalise, balance the other atoms, O and H last. Example: $\ce{Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2}$.

**Half-reaction (ion-electron) method:** write two half-reactions; balance (i) atoms other than O and H, (ii) O with $\ce{H2O}$, (iii) H with $\ce{H+}$, (iv) charge with $\ce{e-}$; multiply to equalise electrons and add. In **basic** medium, add $\ce{OH-}$ equal to the $\ce{H+}$ on both sides and cancel water.

Acidic: $\ce{MnO4- + 8H+ + 5Fe^2+ -> Mn^2+ + 5Fe^3+ + 4H2O}$. Basic: $\ce{2MnO4- + 6I- + 4H2O -> 2MnO2 + 3I2 + 8OH-}$. Always check atoms **and** charge.

key_terms.definition_md: The oxidation or the reduction part of a redox reaction, written with the electrons.
Balancing a redox equation by balancing the two half-reactions separately.

sections.heading: 6. Redox titrations
sections.body_md:
In acid, $\ce{MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- -> Mn^2+ + 4H2O}$, so **1 mol $\ce{MnO4-}$ reacts with 5 mol $\ce{Fe^2+}$**, with 5/2 mol $\ce{H2O2}$, and 5/2 mol $\ce{C2O4^2-}$ ($\ce{2MnO4- + 5C2O4^2- + 16H+ -> 2Mn^2+ + 10CO2 + 8H2O}$). Permanganate is **self-indicating** (end point: first permanent pale pink). Acidify with **dilute sulfuric acid**: hydrochloric acid is oxidised by permanganate and nitric acid is itself an oxidant.

Method: moles of titrant = molarity × volume (L); moles of analyte = moles of titrant × ratio from the balanced equation; molarity = moles ÷ volume of sample (L).

key_terms.definition_md: A reagent whose own colour change signals the end point.
The point at which the titration is stopped, shown here by the first permanent faint pink colour.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Using −2 for oxygen in peroxides, superoxides and OF₂.
- Calling the reduced species the reducing agent (the reducing agent is oxidised).
- Forgetting that the sum of ONs equals the charge, not zero, for an ion.
- Leaving electrons unequal, or H⁺ in a basic-medium equation, or forgetting to check charge.
- Using the ratio 1 : 1 for MnO₄⁻ and Fe²⁺ (it is 1 : 5) or acidifying with HCl.
- Calling every combination or decomposition reaction redox.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: ON of an atom, oxidising or reducing agent, type of reaction.
- Balancing (2–3 marks): the two half-reactions (1), equalised electrons (1), final balanced equation checked for charge (1).
- Titration numericals: balanced ratio (1), moles (1), answer with unit (1).

cards.front_md: Oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons?
cards.back_md: Oxidation: loss of electrons. Reduction: gain of electrons.

cards.front_md: Oxidising agent?
cards.back_md: The species that accepts electrons and is itself reduced.

cards.front_md: Reducing agent?
cards.back_md: The species that donates electrons and is itself oxidised.

cards.front_md: Classical oxidation (oxygen and hydrogen)?
cards.back_md: Addition of oxygen or removal of hydrogen.

cards.front_md: Why do oxidation and reduction occur together?
cards.back_md: Electrons lost by one species must be gained by another.

cards.front_md: What is an oxidation number?

cards.back_md: −1 (it is +1 in most other compounds).

ON of Fe in Fe₃O₄?

cards.back_md: ON has a sign and can be zero or fractional; valence is the number of bonds.

cards.front_md: Which species can only be an oxidising agent?

cards.front_md: Which species can only be a reducing agent?

cards.front_md: Why can H₂O₂ be both oxidant and reductant?

Mole ratio of MnO₄⁻ to Fe²⁺ in acid?

cards.back_md: HCl is oxidised by permanganate and HNO₃ is itself an oxidant; H₂SO₄ is not oxidised.

questions.stem_md: In magnesium pyrophosphate, $\ce{Mg2P2O7}$, the oxidation number of phosphorus is:
In the reaction $\ce{2H2S + SO2 -> 3S + 2H2O}$ the oxidising agent is:

options.text_md: SO₂, because the oxidation number of sulfur falls from +4 to 0
H₂S, because the oxidation number of sulfur falls from −2 to 0
SO₂, because the oxidation number of sulfur rises from +4 to +6

questions.solution_md: Sulfur in H₂S rises from −2 to 0 (oxidised, so H₂S is the reducing agent). Sulfur in SO₂ falls from +4 to 0 (reduced, so SO₂ is the oxidising agent) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Manganese forms the species Mn²⁺, MnO₂, MnO₄²⁻ and MnO₄⁻. Which of them cannot act as a reducing agent?
questions.solution_md: Manganese in MnO₄⁻ is at +7, its highest oxidation state, so it cannot lose more electrons. Mn²⁺ (+2), MnO₂ (+4) and MnO₄²⁻ (+6) can all be oxidised further — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The average oxidation number of iron in magnetite, $\ce{Fe3O4}$, is $+8/3$. This is consistent with a mixture of $\ce{Fe^2+}$ and $\ce{Fe^3+}$ ions in the ratio $\ce{Fe^2+}:\ce{Fe^3+}$ of:
questions.solution_md: For three iron atoms the total is +8. One Fe²⁺ and two Fe³⁺ give 2 + 6 = 8 — option (d). A ratio of 2 : 1 would give 4 + 3 = 7.

questions.stem_md: The oxidation numbers of oxygen in $\ce{BaO2}$, $\ce{KO2}$, $\ce{OF2}$ and $\ce{O3}$, in that order, are:
questions.solution_md: BaO₂ is a peroxide (O at −1); KO₂ is a superoxide, with two O sharing −1 (−½ each); in OF₂ fluorine is more electronegative, so O is +2; ozone is an element, so 0 — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following changes is NOT a redox reaction?
questions.solution_md: The precipitation of barium sulfate changes no oxidation numbers (Ba +2, Cl −1, Na +1, S +6, O −2 throughout). In the other three equations Mg, N, Cu, H, Cl and O change oxidation number — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In the reaction $\ce{2S2O3^2- + I2 -> S4O6^2- + 2I-}$, the average oxidation number of sulfur changes from +2 to:
questions.solution_md: In $\ce{S4O6^2-}$: $4x + 6(-2) = -2$, so $4x = 10$ and $x = +2.5$ — option (d). Sulfur rises, so thiosulfate is the reducing agent and iodine is the oxidising agent.

questions.stem_md: When nitrogen dioxide dissolves in water, $\ce{3NO2 + H2O -> 2HNO3 + NO}$. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: Nitrogen is only reduced, from +4 to +2
Nitrogen is only oxidised, from +4 to +5
Nitrogen is both oxidised (+4 to +5) and reduced (+4 to +2): this is disproportionation
Water is the oxidising agent because its hydrogen is reduced

questions.solution_md: In HNO₃ nitrogen is +5 (a rise of 1) and in NO it is +2 (a fall of 2). One element in one species goes both up and down, so NO₂ disproportionates; water's hydrogen (+1) and oxygen (−2) do not change — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The number of moles of electrons accepted when $1\ \text{mol}$ of $\ce{Cr2O7^2-}$ is reduced to $\ce{Cr^3+}$ in acidic solution is:
questions.solution_md: Each chromium falls from +6 to +3, gaining 3 electrons; two chromium atoms in each Cr₂O₇²⁻ gain 2 × 3 = 6 electrons — option (a). The value 3 is for one chromium atom.

questions.stem_md: In a Daniell cell with a zinc rod in zinc sulfate solution and a copper rod in copper sulfate solution, which statement is correct?

options.text_md: Electrons flow from the copper rod to the zinc rod through the wire, and copper is the anode
Electrons flow through the salt bridge from zinc to copper
Electrons flow from the zinc rod to the copper rod through the external wire, and zinc is the anode
Zinc ions are reduced to zinc at the anode

questions.solution_md: Zinc is the more reactive metal and is oxidised, so it supplies the electrons: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ at the anode. The electrons travel through the wire to the copper cathode where Cu²⁺ is reduced. The salt bridge carries ions, not electrons — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Four metals A, B, C and D were tested with solutions of each other’s sulfates. A displaced C, C displaced B and B displaced D. D did not displace A. The metals in decreasing order of reactivity are:
questions.solution_md: Each displacement tells us that the displacing metal is more reactive: A > C, C > B, B > D. Joining the links gives A > C > B > D — option (b). The failed attempt of D on A agrees with this.

questions.stem_md: Hydrogen peroxide decolourises acidified permanganate solution (oxygen gas is released) but also turns colourless iodide solution brown (iodine forms). These two observations show that:

options.text_md: oxygen in H₂O₂ is at an intermediate oxidation state (−1), so H₂O₂ can act as a reducing agent or an oxidising agent
oxygen in H₂O₂ is at its lowest oxidation state, so H₂O₂ can only reduce
oxygen in H₂O₂ is at its highest oxidation state, so H₂O₂ can only oxidise
H₂O₂ is neither oxidised nor reduced in these reactions

questions.solution_md: Towards permanganate H₂O₂ gives O₂ (oxygen rises from −1 to 0: reducing agent); towards iodide it gives H₂O (oxygen falls from −1 to −2: oxidising agent). Oxygen at −1 lies between −2 and 0 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which formula and Stock name pair is correct?
questions.solution_md: In Fe₂O₃ iron is +3 (2x = 6). FeO has Fe(II), SnCl₄ has Sn(IV) and Cu₂O has Cu(I) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In acidic solution, $\ce{2MnO4- + 5C2O4^2- + 16H+ -> 2Mn^2+ + 10CO2 + 8H2O}$. The amount of permanganate needed to react completely with $0.0050\ \text{mol}$ of ethanedioate (oxalate) ions is:
questions.solution_md: The ratio is 2 mol $\ce{MnO4-}$ to 5 mol $\ce{C2O4^2-}$, so $n(\text{MnO}_4^-) = \dfrac{2}{5} \times 0.0050 = 0.0020\ \text{mol}$ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In which of the following does chlorine have the highest oxidation number?
questions.solution_md: $\ce{Cl2O7}$: $2x - 14 = 0$, so $x = +7$. $\ce{ClO3-}$ is +5, $\ce{ClO2-}$ is +3 and $\ce{ClO-}$ is +1 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: For $\ce{2Al + 3Cu^2+ -> 2Al^3+ + 3Cu}$, the total number of electrons transferred from the reducing agent to the oxidising agent is:
questions.solution_md: Each Al atom loses 3 electrons, so 2 Al lose 6; each Cu²⁺ gains 2, so 3 Cu²⁺ gain 6. The transfer is 6 electrons — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following decomposition reactions is also a redox reaction?
questions.solution_md: Only in HgO decomposition do oxidation numbers change (Hg +2 to 0 and O −2 to 0). In the other three, every element keeps its oxidation number — option (b).

questions.stem_md: At a damp iron surface, rusting involves $\ce{Fe -> Fe^2+ + 2e-}$ and $\ce{O2 + 2H2O + 4e- -> 4OH-}$. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: Iron is reduced and oxygen is oxidised
Oxygen is the reducing agent and iron is the oxidising agent
Iron is oxidised and oxygen is reduced; two iron atoms supply the electrons that one oxygen molecule accepts
Four iron atoms are needed for each oxygen molecule

questions.solution_md: Fe loses electrons (oxidised, the reducing agent) and O₂ gains four electrons (reduced, the oxidising agent). Each Fe gives 2 electrons, so 2 Fe supply the 4 electrons taken by one O₂ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Using the activity series (Mg > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag), which of the following displacement reactions will occur?
questions.solution_md: Only a metal higher in the series displaces one lower down. Iron is above copper, so it displaces copper. Copper is below zinc and magnesium, and silver is below copper, so the other three reactions do not occur — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Chlorate ions are reduced to chloride ions in acid: $\ce{ClO3- + 6H+ -> Cl- + 3H2O}$ (atoms balanced). To balance the charge, how many electrons must be added, and on which side?
questions.solution_md: The left side has charge −1 + 6 = +5 and the right side has −1. Adding 6 electrons (−6) to the left brings it to −1, and a reduction takes electrons in on the reactant side — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Iron(II) solution is acidified with dilute sulfuric acid, not hydrochloric acid, before titration with potassium permanganate. The reason is that:

options.text_md: hydrochloric acid is too weak to supply hydrogen ions
chloride ions would also be oxidised by permanganate, so extra permanganate would be used and the titre would be too high
sulfate ions act as the indicator at the end point
chloride ions would reduce the iron(III) formed back to iron(II)

questions.solution_md: Permanganate oxidises Cl⁻ to Cl₂, consuming titrant that was not used on Fe²⁺, so the titre is too high. Sulfate is not oxidised — option (b). Sulfate plays no part as an indicator, since permanganate is self-indicating.

questions.stem_md: Sulfur occurs in $\ce{H2S}$, $\ce{S8}$, $\ce{SO2}$ and $\ce{H2SO4}$. The oxidation numbers of sulfur in these, in that order, are:
questions.solution_md: H₂S: 2 + x = 0 gives −2. S₈ is an element, so 0. SO₂: x − 4 = 0 gives +4. H₂SO₄: 2 + x − 8 = 0 gives +6 — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Carbon acts as a reducing agent when heated with zinc oxide to give zinc vapour and carbon monoxide.

**Reason (R):** The oxidation number of carbon increases from 0 to +2 in this reaction.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Carbon is oxidised (0 to +2), so it is the reducing agent: A is true. R is also true and is exactly why A holds — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The oxidation number of hydrogen in sodium hydride, NaH, is −1.

**Reason (R):** Hydrogen has oxidation number +1 in hydrogen chloride.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: sodium (+1) is less electronegative than hydrogen, so hydrogen is −1. R is also true, but the +1 state in HCl is a different case and does not explain the −1 in NaH — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Chlorine is reduced when it reacts with potassium bromide solution.

**Reason (R):** The oxidation number of chlorine increases from 0 to −1 in this reaction.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: chlorine goes from 0 to −1 and is reduced, displacing bromine. R is false, because going from 0 to −1 is a decrease, not an increase — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The oxidation number of manganese in potassium manganate, K₂MnO₄, is +7.

**Reason (R):** The oxidation numbers of all atoms in a neutral compound add up to zero.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: In K₂MnO₄: 2(+1) + x + 4(−2) = 0, so x = +6, not +7: A is false. R is a true statement of the sum rule — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Potassium permanganate cannot behave as a reducing agent.

**Reason (R):** Manganese in permanganate is in its highest oxidation state, +7.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Manganese at +7 has no higher state to move to, so it cannot be oxidised: A is true and R explains it — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In a Daniell cell the zinc electrode is the anode.

**Reason (R):** In the external circuit, electrons flow from the copper electrode to the zinc electrode.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Oxidation occurs at zinc, so zinc is the anode: A is true. Electrons flow from zinc to copper in the wire, so R is false — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In $\ce{CrO5}$, which has two peroxide (O–O) groups, chromium has an oxidation number of +10.
questions.solution_md: False. Four oxygens are at −1 (two peroxide groups) and one at −2: x + 4(−1) + (−2) = 0, so chromium is +6; +10 would exceed the number of valence electrons.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Every decomposition reaction is a redox reaction.
questions.solution_md: False. The decomposition of calcium carbonate into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide changes no oxidation number, so it is not redox; decomposition is redox only when oxidation numbers change.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In a redox reaction the total number of electrons lost by the reducing agent equals the total number gained by the oxidising agent.
questions.solution_md: True. Electrons are neither created nor destroyed, so the half-reactions are multiplied until the electrons match.

questions.stem_md: In the half-reaction method for an acidic solution, hydrogen atoms are balanced by adding ___ ions.
questions.solution_md: Oxygen is balanced with water and hydrogen with **H+** (hydrogen ions).

questions.stem_md: In a disproportionation reaction the same element is simultaneously ___ and reduced.
questions.solution_md: One element in one species is both **oxidised** and reduced.

questions.stem_md: The oxidation number of oxygen in potassium superoxide, KO₂, is ___.
questions.solution_md: In KO₂ potassium is +1, so the two oxygen atoms share −1: each is **−1/2**.

questions.stem_md: Match each atom with its oxidation number in the species given.
questions.solution_md: N₂H₄: 2x + 4 = 0, so −2. Na₂S₂O₃: 2 + 2x − 6 = 0, so +2. H₃PO₃: 3 + x − 6 = 0, so +3. HClO₄: 1 + x − 8 = 0, so +7.

questions.stem_md: Match each of these four redox reactions (of nitrogen, sodium nitrate, chlorine and hydrogen peroxide) with the type of redox reaction it shows.
questions.solution_md: Nitrogen and oxygen combine; sodium nitrate decomposes to nitrite and oxygen; chlorine displaces iodine; in hydrogen peroxide oxygen goes from −1 to both −2 and 0.

questions.stem_md: Sodium peroxodisulfate, $\ce{Na2S2O8}$, contains one peroxide (O–O) linkage. Calculate the oxidation number of sulfur in it.
questions.solution_md: Six oxygen atoms are at $-2$ and the two peroxide oxygens are at $-1$: $2(+1) + 2x + 6(-2) + 2(-1) = 0$, so $2x = 12$ and $x = 6$. (Assuming all eight oxygens are $-2$ would wrongly give $+7$.)

marking_scheme.step: Four-term sum with two O at −1

questions.stem_md: Red lead, $\ce{Pb3O4}$, contains lead in the oxidation states +2 and +4. Calculate the average oxidation number of lead.
questions.solution_md: $3x + 4(-2) = 0$, so $3x = 8$ and $x = \dfrac{8}{3} = 2.667 \approx 2.67$. (It is a mixture of two Pb²⁺ and one Pb⁴⁺: $(2 \times 2 + 4)/3$.)

questions.stem_md: A strip of aluminium of mass $2.70\ \text{g}$ dissolves completely in acid to form $\ce{Al^3+}$ ions ($M(\text{Al}) = 27.0\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$, $N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$). Calculate the number of electrons lost by the aluminium, in units of $10^{23}$.
questions.solution_md: $n(\text{Al}) = 2.70/27.0 = 0.100\ \text{mol}$. Each atom loses 3 electrons, so $n(e^-) = 0.100 \times 3 = 0.300\ \text{mol}$ and the number of electrons is $0.300 \times 6.022 = 1.81$ in units of $10^{23}$, that is $1.81 \times 10^{23}$ electrons.

questions.stem_md: $25.0\ \text{mL}$ of an acidified iron(II) sulfate solution needs $18.4\ \text{mL}$ of $0.0200\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ potassium permanganate to reach the end point. Calculate the molarity of the iron(II) solution. ($\ce{MnO4- + 8H+ + 5Fe^2+ -> Mn^2+ + 5Fe^3+ + 4H2O}$)

A student weighs $0.268\ \text{g}$ of sodium ethanedioate, $\ce{Na2C2O4}$ ($M = 134.0\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$), dissolves it in dilute sulfuric acid and titrates it with $0.0200\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ permanganate. ($\ce{2MnO4- + 5C2O4^2- + 16H+ -> 2Mn^2+ + 10CO2 + 8H2O}$) Calculate the volume of permanganate needed, in mL.

A $10.0\ \text{mL}$ sample of hydrogen peroxide solution, acidified with dilute sulfuric acid, needs $22.0\ \text{mL}$ of $0.0200\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ permanganate. ($\ce{2MnO4- + 5H2O2 + 6H+ -> 2Mn^2+ + 5O2 + 8H2O}$) Calculate the molarity of the hydrogen peroxide.

A copper wire is dipped in silver nitrate solution; a grey deposit forms and the solution slowly turns blue. Name the oxidising agent and the reducing agent, and write the half-reaction in which copper is involved.

answer.model_answer_md: Silver ions are the oxidising agent, because they gain electrons and are reduced to silver. Copper is the reducing agent, because it loses electrons. The copper half-reaction is $\ce{Cu -> Cu^2+ + 2e-}$, and the Cu²⁺ ions give the blue colour.

questions.solution_md: Ag⁺ oxidising agent; Cu reducing agent; Cu to Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻.

questions.stem_md: What is the function of the salt bridge in a Daniell cell? What would happen to the current if it were removed?

answer.model_answer_md: The salt bridge allows ions to move between the two half-cells, which keeps each solution electrically neutral and completes the circuit. Without it, charge would build up in each beaker, the circuit would be broken and the current would stop almost at once.

questions.solution_md: Ion movement completes the circuit; without it the current stops.

marking_scheme.step: Ion movement keeps neutrality and completes the circuit

questions.stem_md: Fluorine never shows a positive oxidation number in its compounds, but chlorine can show +1, +3, +5 and +7. Give reasons.

answer.model_answer_md: Fluorine is the most electronegative element, so in every compound it attracts the bonding electrons and has oxidation number −1. Chlorine is less electronegative and, when bonded to more electronegative oxygen or fluorine, it can have positive oxidation numbers, up to +7 with its seven valence electrons.

questions.solution_md: F most electronegative; Cl positive with O and F.

marking_scheme.step: Chlorine positive with more electronegative atoms

questions.stem_md: Define disproportionation. Show with oxidation numbers that the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen is an example.

answer.model_answer_md: Disproportionation is a redox reaction in which one element in a single species is both oxidised and reduced. In $\ce{2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2}$ oxygen is −1 in H₂O₂, falls to −2 in water (reduced) and rises to 0 in oxygen gas (oxidised).

questions.solution_md: Same element oxidised and reduced; O: −1 to −2 and 0.

questions.stem_md: Carbon has a valence of 4 in both methane and methanal, but its oxidation numbers are different. Calculate them and state how the two terms differ.

answer.model_answer_md: In methane, x + 4(+1) = 0 gives −4; in methanal, x + 2(+1) + (−2) = 0 gives 0. Valence is the number of bonds formed and has no sign, so it is 4 in both. Oxidation number is the charge assigned by electronegativity, carries a sign and can be zero or fractional.

questions.solution_md: CH₄: −4; HCHO: 0; valence is unsigned bond count.

questions.stem_md: A zinc granule is dropped into blue copper sulfate solution. The blue colour fades and a reddish-brown solid forms. Explain using half-reactions.

answer.model_answer_md: Zinc loses electrons, $\ce{Zn -> Zn^2+ + 2e-}$, and goes into solution as colourless Zn²⁺. The blue Cu²⁺ ions gain these electrons, $\ce{Cu^2+ + 2e- -> Cu}$, and deposit as reddish-brown copper, so the blue colour fades. Zinc is more reactive than copper.

questions.solution_md: Zn oxidised, Cu²⁺ reduced.

questions.stem_md: Hydrogen peroxide can be used both as a bleach and to remove excess chlorine. Explain with oxidation numbers how the same compound can do both.

answer.model_answer_md: Oxygen in H₂O₂ is at −1, between its lowest state (−2) and 0. As a bleach, it is reduced to water (−2) and so oxidises the dye. With chlorine, it is oxidised to oxygen gas (0) and so reduces Cl₂ to chloride. An intermediate oxidation state allows both.

questions.solution_md: O at −1 can fall to −2 or rise to 0.

marking_scheme.step: Reduced to −2 as bleach; oxidised to 0 with Cl₂

questions.stem_md: Balance $\ce{Zn + HNO3 -> Zn(NO3)2 + N2O + H2O}$ (zinc with dilute nitric acid) by the oxidation-number method.

answer.model_answer_md: Zn rises from 0 to +2, a rise of 2 per atom. N falls from +5 to +1 in N₂O, a fall of 4 per N, so 8 for the two N atoms in one N₂O. Equalising, 4 Zn (rise 8) go with 1 N₂O (fall 8): 4Zn + … → 4Zn(NO₃)₂ + N₂O. Eight nitrate ions go into the salt and two N into N₂O, so ten HNO₃ are used, and hydrogen balance gives five water molecules: $\ce{4Zn + 10HNO3 -> 4Zn(NO3)2 + N2O + 5H2O}$.

questions.solution_md: Rise 2 per Zn; fall 8 per N₂O; 4 : 1; balance N, then H and O.

marking_scheme.step: ON changes of Zn and N

questions.stem_md: Classify each as combination, decomposition, displacement, disproportionation or not redox, giving oxidation-number evidence: (i) $\ce{CaO + SiO2 -> CaSiO3}$; (ii) $\ce{2Al + Fe2O3 -> Al2O3 + 2Fe}$; (iii) $\ce{4KClO3 -> 3KClO4 + KCl}$.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) No oxidation number changes (Ca +2, Si +4, O −2), so it is not redox: a combination of two oxides. (ii) Al rises from 0 to +3 and Fe falls from +3 to 0: a displacement, as aluminium displaces iron. (iii) Chlorine goes from +5 to +7 in KClO₄ and to −1 in KCl: disproportionation, because one element is oxidised and reduced.

questions.solution_md: Not redox; displacement; disproportionation.

questions.stem_md: Balance the disproportionation of bromine in basic solution, $\ce{Br2 -> Br- + BrO3-}$, by the half-reaction method.

answer.model_answer_md: Write the reduction half-reaction first: $\ce{Br2 + 2e- -> 2Br-}$. The oxidation half-reaction, balanced with hydroxide ions because the medium is basic, is $\ce{Br2 + 12OH- -> 2BrO3- + 6H2O + 10e-}$. Multiply the reduction by 5 so that ten electrons are gained and ten are lost, then add the halves: $\ce{6Br2 + 12OH- -> 10Br- + 2BrO3- + 6H2O}$. Every coefficient can be divided by 2 to give $\ce{3Br2 + 6OH- -> 5Br- + BrO3- + 3H2O}$, and the charge is −6 on both sides.

questions.solution_md: Two half-reactions; 5 : 1; halve.

questions.stem_md: In the titration of iron(II) ions with potassium permanganate, (i) why is no indicator added, and (ii) why is the flask acidified with dilute sulfuric acid rather than hydrochloric or nitric acid?

answer.model_answer_md: Permanganate is purple and is reduced to almost colourless Mn²⁺, so the first excess drop gives a faint permanent pink: it is its own indicator. Hydrochloric acid cannot be used because chloride ions are oxidised by permanganate, wasting titrant. Nitric acid is itself an oxidising agent. Sulfate ions are not oxidised, so sulfuric acid is used.

questions.solution_md: Self-indicator; HCl oxidised; HNO₃ oxidant.

(a) State any four rules used to assign oxidation numbers.

(b) Calculate the oxidation number of nitrogen in each ion of $\ce{NH4NO3}$ and of chromium in $\ce{K2Cr2O7}$.

questions.stem_md: Balance $\ce{Cr2O7^2- + SO3^2- -> Cr^3+ + SO4^2-}$ in acidic medium by the half-reaction method. Show each step.

answer.model_answer_md: Reduction half-reaction: balance the two chromium atoms, then add seven water molecules for the seven oxygen atoms, then fourteen hydrogen ions for the hydrogen, and finally six electrons so the charge is +6 on both sides: $\ce{Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6e- -> 2Cr^3+ + 7H2O}$. Oxidation half-reaction: $\ce{SO3^2- + H2O -> SO4^2- + 2H+ + 2e-}$. Multiply the oxidation by 3 so that six electrons are lost, and add the halves. After cancelling six hydrogen ions and three water molecules we obtain $\ce{Cr2O7^2- + 3SO3^2- + 8H+ -> 2Cr^3+ + 3SO4^2- + 4H2O}$, with charge zero on both sides.

questions.stem_md: Balance $\ce{ClO- + CrO2- -> Cl- + CrO4^2-}$ in basic medium by the half-reaction method. Show each step.

answer.model_answer_md: Reduction half-reaction: hypochlorite is reduced to chloride, and in basic medium water is placed on the left and hydroxide on the right: $\ce{ClO- + H2O + 2e- -> Cl- + 2OH-}$. Oxidation half-reaction: $\ce{CrO2- + 4OH- -> CrO4^2- + 2H2O + 3e-}$, balanced first as in acid and then made basic by adding hydroxide ions to cancel the hydrogen ions. Multiply the reduction by 3 and the oxidation by 2 so that six electrons are exchanged, and add the halves. Cancelling three water molecules and six hydroxide ions gives $\ce{3ClO- + 2CrO2- + 2OH- -> 3Cl- + 2CrO4^2- + H2O}$, and the charge is −7 on both sides.

At the copper cathode, reduction occurs: $\ce{Cu^2+ + 2e- -> Cu}$. (c) Electrons flow from zinc to copper through the external wire, because zinc is the stronger reducing agent. (d) The salt bridge lets ions migrate between the beakers, keeping the solutions neutral and completing the circuit.

questions.stem_md: Name the four types of redox reaction. Give one balanced example of each, and show from oxidation numbers why $\ce{CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2}$ is not redox.

answer.model_answer_md: The four types are combination, decomposition, displacement and disproportionation. Combination: $\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$, where nitrogen falls to −3 and hydrogen rises to +1. Decomposition: $\ce{2KClO3 -> 2KCl + 3O2}$, where chlorine falls from +5 to −1 and oxygen rises to 0. Displacement: $\ce{Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu}$, where zinc is oxidised and copper is reduced. Disproportionation: $\ce{2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2}$, where oxygen goes both down to −2 and up to 0. In calcium carbonate, calcium stays +2, carbon stays +4 and oxygen stays −2 in reactants and products, so no electrons are transferred and the reaction is not redox.

questions.solution_md: Four types with examples; no ON change in CaCO₃.
